stories.title_en: Multiple vulnerabilities in Regexp and String case conversion

comments.author: tptacek
comments.text:
There's what I think is probably an awesome bug here.
Windows-1252 encoding has a representation for lowercase German sharp 's' (ß), but not one for the uppercase. If you upcase a string containing a sharp 's', it gets normalized to "SS", which increases the length of the string by one character. The 1252 case conversion code doesn't handle this; it looks like it checks for headroom in the buffer one character at a time. So if the last character of a string you upcase is ß, it looks like you get a one-byte overflow (of 'S').
If that's really the bug (there's a claimed RCE POC), the heap grooming for it must be really fussy! I couldn't find any other character pairs that expand like this.
You can feed strings in 1252 to a Rails program through multipart POSTs, which get to pick their encodings.
The great thing about this bug, apart from how it illustrates how doomed we all are (if I'm right), is that it should by rights have the best vulnerability name of the year, because you get to work 'ß' into it.

comments.author: siscia
comments.text:
I build something similar, based on similar ideas:
https://factory.redbeardlab.com
There is a [language](
https://redbeardlab.github.io/dotFactory/
) that let express complex workflows.
The workflow can be pretty much anything, eg:
1. Clone repo A and B + Start OpenCode + Feed a prompt into it
2. Pick up the commit generated by opencode for both repo, and run CI
Another workflow I created is: every day at 3AM, check that the documentation of the website is up to date, if yes exit, if not update the documentation. Pass the updated documentation to an adversarial LLM and if it pass, merge it - otherwise loop with the feedback from the adversarial one.
You have a concept of trigger, which can be either a webhook, or a github PR or a github issue, or just a cron expression. Or just someone manually clicking.
There is a concept of secrets and config, so the user can create their own secrets to start codex-cloud, or opencode, or making custom API call.
There is also the concept of manual gate, so you can wait for an human to actually click a button.
Finally, it supports running containers. Useful if you want to call an obscure API from your workflow, you don't have to wait for the platfo

comments.text:
It's worth pointing out that there are actually
two
main types of PCMCIA memory cards. The most common by far are the ATA cards mentioned here, which are basically CF cards in a different form factor (equivalent to a CF card in a CF-to-PCMCIA adapter) and work by emulating either an IDE hard drive or an ISA IDE controller depending on wiring. While uncommon at this point, CF controller chips are still available and some specialized suppliers do manufacture these cards brand new using modern NAND flash.
The much more problematic ones to find a replacement for in 2026 are the so-called "linear" memory-mapped cards, consisting of one or more banks of raw parallel NOR flash with no controller IC. Linear cards were never standardized and the protocol used to interface to parallel flash can vary greatly across chip families, so the vast majority of devices that use them are hardcoded to only accept cards with a specific manufacturer and device ID.
